Shir Ali Khan repeatedly climbed the fortress wall and attempted to plant the victory flag.
Shir Ali Khan received a robe of honor and decoration for bravery.
Rashid Khan, a colonel of the Mokhberan regiment, was wounded in the leg during the Herat fighting.
Nabi Khan died shortly after being removed from the battlefield with severe wounds.
Nabi Khan was transferred with other Gharagozloo dead for burial in Mashhad by order of Mohammad Shah.
Mahmoud Khan was the son of Nabi Khan and a descendant of Mohammad Hossein Khan Ashiqloo.
The Gharagozloo guard defending Bushehr numbered fifty soldiers.
British forces dispersed the small Gharagozloo guard and occupied Bushehr to pressure Iran over Herat.
Gharagozloo troops helped assault the Herat fortifications and open the fortress gates.
Mahmoud Khan Gharagozloo argued for peace in a state consultation during the Anglo-Persian crisis.

object_text: At Bandar Lengeh, Mostafa Qoli Khan Mirpanj tried to prevent a British ship carrying prisoners from departing; he exchanged fire with two guns and withdrew inland.
Rustam Khan joined the southern Iranian forces with artillery during the Anglo-Persian War.
Ali Khan received a superficial wound to the arm during fighting against British forces.
Two soldiers of the Gharagozloo special regiment and one of the fourth regiment were captured and later released in Bushehr.
Ali Naqi Khan led the Dargazin infantry regiment and defeated Nasrallah Khan of Laristan in Bikhuh district.
Ali Khan Nosrat al-Molk served as first-rank sartip responsible for order in Kerman in 1277 AH.
Ali Khan and his troops drilled daily in the Kerman citadel square and joined the expedition against Azad Khan Kharani.
Mohammad Hossein Khan, son of Ali Khan, received the title Hosam al-Molk in 1287 AH for service in Kerman.
Zeyn al-Abedin Khan arranged the marriage of his son Gholamreza Khan to Qamar al-Saltaneh in 1309 AH.
The wedding celebrations lasted about one month and reportedly cost more than one hundred thousand tomans.
Hosam al-Molk, Saed al-Saltaneh, and Zia al-Molk were dismissed and detained after being blamed for the Hamadan unrest.
Hosam al-Molk offered 100,000 tomans for the governments of Hamadan, Borujerd, and Luristan, then 80,000 tomans to the shah and 20,000 to Amin al-Soltan for Kerman.
Hosam al-Molk was appointed governor of Kermanshah on 12 Rabi I 1311 AH.
Aqa Jan Gharagozloo held the rank of yavar.
Aqa Jan fled after Pavlov’s death, was captured in Hamadan, imprisoned in Tehran, and handed to the Russian embassy.
Seven or eight people were killed during the confrontation between Gharagozloo forces and residents of Shiraz.
Mahmoud Khan was the son of Nabi Khan and a descendant of Mohammad Hossein Khan of the Ashiqloo branch.
After Nabi Khan’s death in the Herat campaign, Mahmoud Khan was placed in command of his father’s troops.
Mahmoud Khan served as deputy governor of Hamadan and the Gharagozloo districts during the late reign of Fath Ali Shah.
Mahmoud Khan received authority over Darjazin, Jahraman, Tohidlu, and the districts attached to Khan Baba Khan in 1246-1247 AH.
Mahmoud Khan was appointed colonel in 1254 AH and promoted to sartip in 1255 AH.
Mahmoud Khan was appointed Iranian envoy to Russia in 1269 AH.
After returning from Saint Petersburg in 1272 AH, Mahmoud Khan was promoted to mirpanj and received a royal robe.
Mahmoud Khan later held senior posts including foreign affairs, war, state buildings, and government papers administration.
Mahmoud Khan imported approximately 90,000 tomans of machinery from Moscow for a steam-powered spinning factory, but the project failed because trained personnel were unavailable.
Mahmoud Khan became the first minister of commerce when that ministry was established in 1277 AH.
Abdollah Khan Sarem al-Saltaneh died in Dhu al-Qada 1278 AH.

Amir Afkham assisted Russian forces in occupying Hamadan and became governor under Russian protection.

object_text: The Gharagozloos were Turkic-speaking and belonged under the Bigdili grouping, described as one of the twenty-four major Oghuz tribes.
After the Mongol invasion, the Gharagozloos moved west toward Syria, joined other Turkic groups, and became associated with the Shamlu confederation.
Timur moved them eastward; they later settled again on the Iranian plateau and entered the Safavid Qizilbash confederation.
Under Shah Abbas and in the late Safavid period, the Gharagozloos regained prominence and their presence around Hamadan became clear.
Under the Qajars they gained exceptional trust, culminating in Naser al-Molk Gharagozloo’s selection as regent after the death of Azod al-Molk.
The tribe provided extensive military service across Iran but was later marginalized as the Qajar order declined.
The chapter identifies Hajilu, Ashiqloo, and Uzbeklu as principal Gharagozloo branches, while treating claims of absorption or renaming cautiously.
Landed property and agricultural production formed a major economic base of Gharagozloo elite power in Hamadan.
Military strength, alongside landed wealth, was a principal basis of Gharagozloo prominence under the Qajars.
The Sixth, Mansur, Mokhberan, and Fadavi regiments are identified as four principal Gharagozloo military formations.
Regimental command was not rigidly confined by tribal branch; cross-branch and external appointments occurred.
Formal rules against purchasing military office diverged from practice, as illustrated by payments for rank and command.
The author favors an Oghuz-Turkic origin and considers a connection through Bigdili and Shamlu plausible.
notes: Author synthesis; organizational affiliation, not a biological genealogy.

object_text: The theory that the Gharagozloos first entered Iran as a Mongol-period group is discussed but rejected by the author.
notes: Rejected hypothesis preserved for historiographical transparency.

object_text: Several earlier writers describe the Gharagozloos as a branch or remnant of the Shamlu.
The book describes the Gharagozloos as joining or belonging to the Qizilbash political-military world by the late fifteenth or early Safavid period.
It is uncertain whether Amir Jafar Ali Gharagoz belonged to the same Gharagozloo grouping later prominent in Hamadan.
Amir Mohammad Gharagoz may represent continued Gharagozloo service among Timurid or Mughal forces, but the identification is not conclusive.
Gharagozloo figures held military, court, and provincial offices under the Safavids.
By the eighteenth century the Gharagozloos possessed significant landed and military power in the Hamadan region.
The Gharagozloos became important allies of Karim Khan Zand and participated in campaigns against his rivals.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar preserves an older family genealogy running through Qara Mohammad, Haji Bonyad Khan, Haji Qasem, Haji Jafar Khan and Haji Abdollah Beg before the later Hajilou line.
notes: This is a transmitted family-genealogy tradition. Do not assume Majmooe Asaar's Haji Jafar Khan is identical with P0094 without separate identity reconciliation.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar explicitly enumerates Haji Fathollah as a sixth son of Haji Abdollah Beg.
notes: Source-explicit statement preserved as evidence; v2.8.0 canonical topology currently has five branch heads and is intentionally unchanged.

object_text: Haji Fathollah is described as not entering government service and as occupying himself with landed/property affairs together with Haji Safar Khan.
notes: Claim concerns the source's description of Haji Fathollah, not canonical identity placement.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar names Abbas Beg, Allah-Panah Beg and Heidar Qoli Beg as children of Haji Fathollah.
notes: Names retained as source-derived candidates; no person records or parent_of edges created yet.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar lists six sons: Mohammad Baqer Khan, Haji Hamze Khan, Haji Ali Mohammad Khan, Mehdi Khan Sartip, Zolfaghar Khan and Mohammad Qoli Khan.
notes: Alternate source list differs from the current canonical v2.8.0 child set. Mohammad Qoli may correspond to Haji Yavar Mohammad Gholi, but that identity is not proven.

Mehdi Khan Sartip is named by Majmooe Asaar as a son of Haji Mohammad Khan Jeyhunabadi.
Majmooe Asaar's Mohammad Qoli Khan may be the same person as the canonical Haji Yavar Mohammad Gholi, but the identification is not yet demonstrated.

Majmooe Asaar names Haji Mirza Safi Qoli Khan, Haji Abolqasem Khan, Haji Morteza Qoli Khan, Mohammad Ali Khan, Hossein Ali Beg and Mehdi Qoli Beg in the Haji Mina branch.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar describes Nasrollah Khan as commander of the Hajilou cavalry.
Majmooe Asaar says Nasrollah Khan often served in Shiraz under Hasan Ali Mirza Farmanfarma.
Majmooe Asaar names seven children of Nasrollah Khan: Ghaffar Khan, Mirza Hashem Khan, Mohammad Hossein Khan, Qasem Khan, Hassan Khan, Abdollah Khan and Nasir Beg.
notes: Source-explicit child list; no canonical child nodes or edges are added in this evidence checkpoint.

object_text: Abdollah Khan Amir Nezam served on a government frontier assignment at Sarakhs/Naseriyeh from approximately 1294 to 1296 AH.
notes: Mission chronology from the editor's introduction and Kitabche-ye Merv opening.

object_text: Abdollah Khan authored the Report on Sarakhs and Naseriyeh Fortress, completed or dated 1296 AH.
During the Sarakhs mission Abdollah Khan is identified as a colonel (sarhang) of the Fadavi Regiment.
notes: Structured military-command linkage should be added only after exact current military-unit/organization IDs are reconciled.

object_text: At Naseriyeh soldiers performed night guard while also undertaking daytime duties involving water works, fuel collection, patrols and response to Turkmen incursions.
Fuel scarcity forced soldiers to leave the fortress several times each month to collect firewood, and weaker soldiers sometimes purchased it at high prices from Turkmen suppliers.
Abdollah Khan judged service at Sarakhs to be harder on soldiers than service at Iran's other frontiers because they were rarely free from duty.
notes: Explicit contemporary assessment by the author.

object_text: Abdollah Khan proposed replacing two hundred subsidized kharalchi households with twenty-seven useful cavalrymen as a more effective use of state resources.
notes: Author's reform proposal; preserve as his judgment.

object_text: Abdollah Khan proposed expanding local cultivation and reducing dependence on government grain rations, with produce valued against official Mashhad grain prices.
Abdollah Khan described Naseriyeh as a strongly built fortified settlement with houses, a bazaar and multiple defensive works.
notes: Avoid normalizing uncertain architectural headcounts and dimensions until visually rechecked.

object_text: Naseriyeh functioned as both a rotating military garrison and a settlement containing permanently resident military households with wives and children.
notes: Exact roster numbers remain a separate research question.

object_text: Qal'eh Now was described as a small fort about one-quarter farsakh above Sarakhs with a permanent garrison of twenty-five soldiers.
notes: Source-stated historical distance retained without modern conversion.

object_text: Qal'eh Now protected workers maintaining the Sarakhs river dam and irrigation works, giving them a refuge in case of attack.
Qal'eh Qassab was described as an old uninhabited ruin approximately one and one-half farsakhs above Sarakhs.
notes: Source-stated historical distance retained without modern conversion.

object_text: The ruined Qushid Khan Fortress near Sarakhs was associated in Abdollah Khan's account with the Teke leader Qushid Khan and an earlier Teke presence.
notes: Historical association reported in Kitabche-ye Merv/Sarakhs material.

object_text: Sarakhs garrison operations depended on river-control infrastructure, and large numbers of soldiers could be required to rebuild or maintain diversion works when water was low.
notes: Firsthand observation; exact workforce figures should remain source-attributed.

object_text: During Abdollah Khan's two-year stay, Sarakhs experienced periods when river water failed to reach the settlement and residents relied on wells.
Abdollah Khan recommended construction of one or more cisterns to provide a more reliable reserve when river water was interrupted.
Abdollah Khan described Sarakhs soil as highly fertile, with abundant melons and watermelons, productive wheat and repeated alfalfa harvests.
notes: Combines his observation with local testimony; historical yield ratios are intentionally not normalized here.

object_text: During his Sarakhs service Abdollah Khan deliberately investigated the conditions, customs, population and life of Turkmen communities around Merv and Sarakhs and compiled the Kitabche-ye Merv.
notes: Purpose statement at the beginning of Kitabche-ye Merv.

object_text: Abdollah Khan explicitly cautioned that Turkmen tribal histories were transmitted orally and could not be regarded as fully reliable; he therefore questioned elders he considered comparatively trustworthy.
notes: Important statement about the evidence basis of the historical/tribal narrative.

object_text: The Kitabche-ye Merv reports that Salur groups supplied Iranian government forces with provisions and furnished about five hundred cavalry.
notes: Historical testimony from informants, not Abdollah Khan's eyewitness observation.

object_text: The source reports that Salur households were relocated under Iranian government support to Old Sarakhs, while about five hundred households remained at Zurabad.
notes: Source-stated household count and relocation narrative.

object_text: The Qara'i Regiment was garrisoning Naseriyeh Fortress during the Salur relocation episode described in Kitabche-ye Merv.
notes: Historical narrative; structured military-unit link deferred pending current unit-ID reconciliation.

object_text: About six months after the Salur gathered at Sarakhs, the source says Qushid Khan sent approximately three thousand cavalry and infantry under Khajqa Sardar against them.
notes: Approximate force size and names are source-attributed historical testimony.

object_text: Khajqa Sardar's force seized Salur livestock and compelled the Salur to leave Sarakhs for Merv, where they lived among the Teke.

The same account says the displaced Salur families were protected during the journey and their livestock was restored, while also portraying their later condition among the Teke as subordinate and impoverished.
notes: Preserves the source's internally complex portrayal rather than flattening it.

object_text: In Abdollah Khan's transmitted historical account, Abbas Mirza's Sarakhs campaign freed about three thousand Shiite captives and resulted in about five thousand Turkmen captives being taken toward Mashhad.
notes: These are source-reported figures from a non-eyewitness historical narrative and are not independently verified here.

object_text: Abdollah Khan served in Khuzestan for approximately two and a half years during the 1305–1308 AH period and documented the mission in a dedicated report.
The Fadavi Regiment reached Khuzestan before Nezam al-Saltaneh and initially camped outside Dezful.
During the Falahiyah crisis the Fadavi Regiment marched in extreme summer heat, remained at Falahiyah about two months, and then moved toward Ahvaz and Hoveyzeh.
Abdollah Khan described Falahiyah as exceptionally hot and oppressive, with severe humid sharji conditions, hot winds and dangerous scorpions.
notes: Authorial observation; source-stated temperature measurements are not normalized here.

object_text: After order was restored, four detachments were left as garrisons in Falahiyah and Hoveyzeh while most of the regiment returned to Shushtar.
Before the New Year, one hundred soldiers and fifty military musicians accompanied Nezam al-Saltaneh toward Mohammerah.
Abdollah Khan described Dezful as comparatively prosperous and reported about three hundred shops, five caravanserais and ten bathhouses.
Merchants of Dezful and Shushtar maintained commercial relationships extending to Bombay/India and traded goods including wool, borage, lambskins and opium.
notes: Trade geography reported by Abdollah Khan.

object_text: Abdollah Khan described the Dezful bridge as having twenty-one major arches and reported a partial collapse that temporarily forced travelers to cross by raft.
notes: Historical measurements and condition should remain source-attributed.

object_text: Shush and the shrine of the Prophet Daniel were described as approximately four farsakhs from Dezful.
Govanak was an intermediate stage on the Dezful–Shushtar road, with saline water and Bakhtiari Chahar-Lang residents.
Abdollah Khan gave the Dezful–Shushtar road as approximately ten farsakhs and described a stretch beyond Govanak with no fresh water.
At Shushtar the river system divided into the Shatit and Karun branches as described by Abdollah Khan.
Abdollah Khan estimated Shushtar at roughly four thousand households and about twenty-two thousand people.
The report records twenty-one old muzzle-loading guns at Shushtar, many without carriages, with some repaired for operations toward Falahiyah and Ahvaz.
At Ahvaz Abdollah Khan recommended staged canal development before committing the state to full reconstruction of the old dam.
Abdollah Khan estimated that full reconstruction of the Ahvaz dam and related canals might cost more than one hundred fifty thousand tomans.
Abdollah Khan criticized delays caused by shipping through Basra before Mohammerah and advocated more direct, formal port procedures at Mohammerah/Sahebqaraniyeh.
Falahiyah was described as roughly five hundred households with about one hundred shops and commercial ties to Shushtar and Mohammerah.
At Nezam al-Saltaneh's arrival, Sheikh Abdollah Khan was described as exercising effectively independent authority in Falahiyah.
notes: Political situation as reported by Abdollah Khan.

object_text: The government first attempted to mediate the Falahiyah dispute and dispatched two detachments of Chaharmahal troops with an Austrian mountain gun.
After the mediation failed and government forces approached, Sheikh Abdollah Khan withdrew toward Mohammerah and local sheikhs accepted Sheikh Ja'far Khan's authority.
Abdollah Khan judged Sheikh Ja'far Khan highly capable and particularly suitable for governing Falahiyah.
notes: Explicit authorial judgment, not a neutral fact.

object_text: Abdollah Khan described the government of Hoveyzeh as historically associated with descendants of Sayyid Mohammad ibn Falah.
During Nezam al-Saltaneh's administration, Mowla Nasrollah Khan was assigned Hoveyzeh and associated territories for an annual fiscal obligation reported as six thousand tomans.
Abdollah Khan regarded Mowla Motalleb Khan's prestige among Arab groups as useful political leverage over the Bani Torof even when he was out of office.
Abdollah Khan described the Bani Torof as controlling important fertile lands and regarded excessive growth of their political power as a problem requiring balance.
The Bani Saleh were described as a tent-dwelling group cultivating dry-farmed lands south of Hoveyzeh and grazing seasonally between the Karkheh River and Hoveyzeh.
The report names Mahudar, Haji Ne'mat and Mahawi as leaders associated with the Bani Saleh.
notes: Names preserved from source; normalized transliteration remains open.

object_text: The report attributes approximately fifteen hundred mounted men and riflemen to the Bani Saleh.
The Bani Saleh passage contains apparently inconsistent household figures that should not be normalized until visually reconciled.
notes: Evidence-quality flag retained in claim layer.

object_text: Across the Khuzestan report Abdollah Khan repeatedly evaluated roads, water, military readiness, settlement, agriculture, trade and local political authority as interdependent parts of provincial administration.
notes: Interpretive synthesis grounded in multiple explicit recommendations; not a direct quotation.

object_text: In 1309 AH Abdollah Khan went to Shiraz with the Fadavi Regiment and was assigned responsibility for guarding Shiraz and its citadel.
In 1310 AH Abdollah Khan was drawn into the Molla Abdollah Borujerdi crisis, summoned to Tehran, imprisoned and put in chains.
notes: The fact of detention is secure; sources differ on motive and political framing.

object_text: A source cited in the historical literature records a 7,000-toman payment associated with Abdollah Khan's release after the 1310 AH detention.
notes: Preserve as source-reported financial outcome, not a fully reconstructed legal judgment.

object_text: Within months of the 1310 AH imprisonment Abdollah Khan was restored to command and appointed to lead the Fars forces.
In Ramadan 1311 AH Abdollah Khan became deputy governor of Fars after Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi's removal.
The source reports roughly seven or eight deaths during the Shiraz confrontation involving Abdollah Khan's regiment.
notes: Historical source estimate; do not normalize beyond the stated range.

object_text: In Dhu al-Qa'dah 1314 AH Abdollah Khan Sardar Akram became governor and military head of Khuzestan, replacing Ahmad Khan Ala al-Dowleh.
notes: Editor and later Gharagozloo history corroborate this appointment.

object_text: At the time of the 1314 AH Khuzestan appointment, Hossein Qoli Khan received his father's former title Sa'ed al-Saltaneh and Mohtaj Ali Khan received Ejlal al-Mamalek.
notes: Title transfers are source-reported; no genealogy changes.

object_text: A jeweled sword was reportedly awarded to Abdollah Khan in 1316 AH in recognition of his Khuzestan service.
notes: Corroborated in the Gharagozloo history; retained here as a mature-career honor claim.

object_text: Later sources portray Abdollah Khan as a major landholder, with a source-stated figure of roughly 120 villages/properties across Hamadan, Arak and Khamseh late in life.
notes: The aggregate number should remain a historical estimate until estate-by-estate reconstruction.

object_text: A report preserved by the editor portrays Abdollah Khan Sardar Akram as strongly opposed to the early Majles and constitutional movement in 1324 AH.
notes: Time-bounded political position; do not treat as immutable lifelong identity.

object_text: During a Hamadan grain crisis, townspeople and officials accused Abdollah Khan and other major khans of withholding grain.
notes: Accusation preserved as accusation, not established guilt.

object_text: Abdollah Khan later wrote to his steward indicating that he did not approve of hoarding grain.
In Muharram 1325 AH Abdollah Khan's Amir Noyan/Sardar Akram command was abolished and his Fars military salary was stopped.
In Safar 1325 AH Abdollah Khan was nominated to govern Kurdistan, but the Majles blocked the appointment.
On 27 Rabi II 1326 AH a Fadavi Regiment wage protest led to Abdollah Khan's War Ministry questioning and dismissal from government office.
After Mohammad Ali Shah's coup against the constitutional order, Abdollah Khan was restored to royal favor and granted the title Amir Nezam.
In Ramadan 1326 AH Abdollah Khan Amir Nezam commanded Hamadan regiments in the royalist campaign against constitutionalist Tabriz.
notes: Politically sensitive event stated without advocacy.

object_text: Abdollah Khan served as Minister of Finance in 1327 AH and later again in the Ayn al-Dowleh cabinet in 1333 AH.
Mohammad Mosaddegh later criticized Amir Nezam's competence as finance minister and alleged that he used divination when considering appointments.
notes: Retrospective criticism attributed to Mosaddegh, not adopted as archive judgment.

object_text: The editor identifies Abdollah Khan as governor of Kurdistan by 1328 AH, though the exact start date is uncertain.

In 1328 AH officials investigated excavations on Abdollah Khan's Kordabad property; reports accused him of extensive digging for antiquities, while he claimed to have purchased government authorization for 3,000 tomans.
notes: Investigation and competing claims preserved; no finding of guilt asserted.

object_text: During the Salar al-Dowleh crisis around 1330 AH Abdollah Khan first associated his force with Salar al-Dowleh while remaining somewhat separate, then joined government forces under Farmanfarma after Salar retreated.
notes: Sequence preserved separately from the editor's harsher interpretation.

object_text: On 28 Rajab 1332 AH Abdollah Khan was elected as one of Hamadan's deputies to the Third Majles with a source-reported 4,829 votes.
notes: Major political reversal from earlier anti-Majles stance.

object_text: Abdollah Khan died on Sunday, 23 Sha'ban 1334 AH (1916 CE), after a partial stroke while the First World War had reached Hamadan.
Abdollah Khan's later career moved from early opposition to the constitutional movement and royalist military service to eventual election as a Third Majles deputy.
notes: Archive synthesis derived from dated events; not a direct quotation.

object_text: Abdollah Khan undertook a Mecca pilgrimage in 1319 AH and left a surviving first-person travelogue of the journey.
Abdollah Khan compared alternative routes from Baku toward Istanbul via Tiflis/Batum and northern Black Sea connections, weighing time, price and comfort.
The diary describes an integrated Istanbul-to-Jeddah ticket using ship travel to Alexandria, rail transport through Egypt toward Suez, and ship travel from Suez to Jeddah.
Abdollah Khan recorded railway distance, stages and class-based fares on the Alexandria/Egypt–Suez corridor, including Ismailia.
On approaching Jeddah the diary describes dangerous rocky waters and a local pilot boarding the vessel to guide it safely into anchorage.
Abdollah Khan accused the Iranian consular establishment associated with Jeddah of repeated fee extraction from Iranian pilgrims through passport, transport and related charges.
notes: Confirmed as an accusation made by the author; the underlying misconduct is not independently adjudicated here.

object_text: Abdollah Khan alleged that belongings of Iranian pilgrims who died could be taken into consular control in ways he regarded as abusive.
notes: Authorial accusation, not independent finding of misconduct.

object_text: Abdollah Khan argued that Iranian pilgrims might be better served without the existing Jeddah consular arrangement and favored more direct dealings with the Sharif of Mecca.
Abdollah Khan estimated Mecca's population at approximately eighty thousand.
Abdollah Khan described many Meccan houses as multi-story stone-and-plaster buildings and compared aspects of their form with buildings he had seen elsewhere.
Abdollah Khan strongly criticized street sanitation in Mecca and reported raising the issue with the Sharif.
A severe cholera outbreak in Mecca during Dhu al-Hijjah 1319 AH altered the plans of many pilgrims and Abdollah Khan's own onward travel decisions.
Abdollah Khan records using estekhareh when deciding whether to continue toward Medina during the cholera outbreak.
notes: Direct self-report; this independently demonstrates personal use of estekhareh in travel decisions.

object_text: On 14 Dhu al-Hijjah 1319 AH Abdollah Khan reported seeing roughly fifty dead people along the road as cholera worsened.
On 15 Dhu al-Hijjah Abdollah Khan's planned departure was delayed because transport animals could not be obtained.
Abdollah Khan's wife died in Mecca on 15 Dhu al-Hijjah 1319 AH after severe illness during the pilgrimage.
notes: Editor notes indicate pre-existing heart palpitations and worsening illness amid cholera and heat; her personal identity remains unresolved.

object_text: During the final days in Mecca Abdollah Khan records performing devotional acts on behalf of the Shah, Atabak-e A'zam, Sepahsalar, his father, his mother and the late Haji Mohammad Khan.
notes: First-person diary; preserve as religious/personal practice.

object_text: Before meeting the Sharif of Mecca Abdollah Khan was told that custom required kissing the Sharif's hand; he explicitly refused and entered without doing so.
notes: First-person account of his own conduct.

object_text: During the meeting with the Sharif, Abdollah Khan raised concerns about pilgrim treatment and expressed appreciation for comparatively favorable treatment of Shi'i pilgrims.
The closing diary entries record visits to the cemetery associated with Abu Talib and sites connected with Amina, Khadija, Abd al-Muttalib and Abd Manaf.
The surviving Mecca travelogue does not provide a complete return-home itinerary after the final Mecca entries.
Abdollah Khan's surviving writings refer retrospectively to earlier European travel, including Rome, Paris, St. Petersburg and Moscow.
notes: Retrospective reference only; no full Europe diary is currently present in the source collection.

object_text: The surviving writings/editorial synthesis report that Abdollah Khan referred to having met the King of Italy.
notes: Preserve as retrospective self-reference/editorial synthesis until the original Europe diary is located.

object_text: The editor states that Abdollah Khan referred to a separate European travelogue, but that work was not among the eight writings located and published in Majmooe Asaar.
notes: Source-preservation fact; do not treat the missing travelogue as directly available evidence.

object_text: The Mecca travelogue shows Abdollah Khan repeatedly comparing transport systems, prices, urban form, administration and public services across multiple countries and cities.
notes: Archive synthesis based on multiple direct observations; not a quotation.

object_text: Abdollah Khan authored Kitabcheh-ye Merv, a distinct report completed in 1296 AH.
notes: Keep distinct from the Sarakhs/Naseriyeh report.

object_text: The Merv booklet associates major Teke groupings with Aqtemish and Taqtemish branches and with Merv and Akhal.
The source associates Araz Khan with building Qarli Band on the Tejen.
The source links Qarli Band irrigation with expanded cultivation and improved grain prosperity.
Khvajam Shokur Aq-Saqal is described as an influential leader associated with movement of Teke groups between Tejen and Sarakhs.
The source says roughly six thousand households eventually gathered under Khvajam Shokur's authority.
Abdollah Khan portrays Khvajam Shokur as exercising severe coercive authority over trade and internal discipline.
notes: Authorial portrayal; not neutral character judgment.

object_text: Qushid Khan is described as having been selected as commander during a major conflict involving Turkmen groups and Khiva.
The source associates Qushid Khan with building the fortress later bearing his name near Sarakhs.
notes: Person-place association retained in claim layer pending person-ID reconciliation.

object_text: Mohammad Amin Khan of Khiva advanced from the Merv region toward Sarakhs and surrounded the Teke defensive concentration at Qushid Khan's fortress.
Before the fighting, the Teke reportedly attempted submission through gifts of money and horses, which Mohammad Amin Khan rejected.
The source names Aman Sa'd Sardar and Bardi Niyaz Khan, son of Araz Khan, among Teke commanders during the battle.
notes: Names preserved from source; transliteration may need later normalization.

object_text: The source says Mohammad Amin Khan of Khiva was killed during the battle near Sarakhs.
notes: Historical claim as reported by Abdollah Khan.

object_text: Mir Ahmad Khan Jamshidi is described as reorganizing the surviving Khivan army and withdrawing it in good order.
After Qushid Khan's death, the source says no single Merv khan was accepted by the entire Teke population.
The source identifies Araz Morad Khan, Beg Morad Khan, Baba Khan son of Qushid Khan, and Nur Verdi Khan among the principal chiefs in the fragmented leadership structure.
Abdollah Khan judges Nur Verdi Khan and Beg Morad Khan favorably while describing Baba Khan very negatively.
notes: Explicit authorial assessment, not neutral personality fact.

object_text: The Merv economy is described as highly dependent on river and dam irrigation, with major disorder when the dam failed.
The source describes mobilization of several thousand workers to repair damaged irrigation infrastructure.
The source describes strong production of melons, watermelons, pumpkins, grains and other field crops, while fruit gardens were relatively scarce.
Camel-thorn shrubs and tamarisk are described as important fuel sources, with winter fuel stockpiling.
The source reports two weekly markets, on Mondays and Thursdays, near Qushid Khan's house in the Taqtamish area.
Abdollah Khan estimates that large cash fortunes were uncommon among the Teke population of Merv.
notes: Authorial estimate; do not convert into modern wealth statistics.

object_text: Abdollah Khan argues that Teke cavalry numbers had declined and that assembling even ten thousand mounted men would have been difficult in his time.
Abdollah Khan describes Teke rifle infantry as formidable, including prone firing and an effective range he reports at around three hundred paces.
The source uses the term mirkan for the type of Teke rifleman being described.
The source portrays Salur communities in Merv as politically and economically subordinate to Teke power, including limited land and water autonomy.
Abdollah Khan describes social barriers around intermarriage between Salur and Teke groups, while noting that wealth could sometimes override them.
notes: Historical social observation, not timeless generalization.

object_text: In the Merv booklet Abdollah Khan combines political history, ethnography, warfare, irrigation, agriculture, markets, wealth and military analysis in one regional report.
notes: Archive synthesis derived from the work's structure.

object_text: Majmooe Asaar preserves three distinct Kalat Naderi reports by Abdollah Khan, including a 1302 AH strategic report and a separate repair-inspection booklet.
Abdollah Khan estimated that Kalat could internally sustain roughly six thousand sheep without outside pasture.
Abdollah Khan estimated that Kalat could internally sustain roughly five hundred mares.
The source reports actual sheep holdings around twelve thousand.
The report describes prolonged seasonal pasture availability in Kalat's mountain and valley environment.
Brushwood from Shir Kuh and other local mountain vegetation served as major fuel resources.
The report describes substantial wild pistachio growth in areas behind the Kalat mountains.
Abdollah Khan describes abundant Maku'i cumin in and around Kalat.
Abdollah Khan argues that organized cumin collection could potentially cover Kalat's entire tax obligation.
notes: Authorial economic assessment, not audited fiscal fact.

object_text: Abdollah Khan believed local inhabitants could profit more from resources then being harvested seasonally by outsiders from Tabas near Kashtani and Chub Mast.
notes: Authorial economic recommendation; botanical term remains unresolved.

object_text: The report argues that Kalat's internal food production could provision a population around ten thousand even though far fewer soldiers should be needed for defense.
Abdollah Khan considered Kalat unusually defensible because water and provisions could be produced within the fortified region.
Report 2 identifies five principal entrances suitable for routine passage of men and horses.
Report 2 describes approximately seventy-five additional pedestrian routes, several of which could also admit horses.
notes: Survey estimate before more detailed repair inspection.

object_text: Abdollah Khan authored a distinct treatise analyzing taxation and provincial fiscal administration in Fars.
The treatise analyzes revenue movement through a chain of central government, provincial governor, subordinate officials or tribal authorities, and cultivators/households.
Abdollah Khan argues that appointing an intelligent or just governor is insufficient unless relationships among fiscal layers are formally bounded and defined.
The treatise distinguishes landed/arbabi tax systems from khalesegi and tribal fiscal systems.
In landed-property systems, Abdollah Khan says abuse more often entered through bribes, gifts, fines and fabricated charges than through formal reassessment known to landowners.
The Darab example gives tax plus tafavot-e amal at roughly twenty-seven thousand tomans.
Abdollah Khan argues that cutting the provincial demand on Darab would not automatically reduce what cultivators paid; the benefit could be retained by the district governor.
Qir-o Karzin, Laristan, Darab and Behbahan are among districts cited in discussion of khalesegi-style fiscal arrangements.
The treatise discusses customary agricultural shares such as ushr and khoms, and in some contexts fixed dues associated with productive assets such as date palms.
Abdollah Khan compares some local revenue arrangements to leasing, where an administrator committed to pay above the formal assessment and sought profit through greater cultivation/output.
He argues that a customary one-tenth levy should not simply be converted to one-fifth under the pretext of raising more revenue.
Qashqai, Arab and Baharlu groups are explicitly cited in discussion of tribal household taxation through kadkhodas and subordinate chiefs.
Abdollah Khan argues that reducing state demands on tribal leadership would not necessarily reduce what ordinary tribal households paid.
The source identifies Haji Rostam Khan as son of Fath Ali Khan Lari in the Laristan fiscal example.
notes: Do not create canonical person record until identity reconciliation.

object_text: The source reports roughly thirty-two thousand tomans paid to the Fars government as tafavot-e amal in the Laristan example.
Abdollah Khan uses the Laristan case to argue that shifting revenue between the provincial governor and local administrator does not necessarily benefit cultivators.
Abdollah Khan distinguishes customary principal and supplementary fiscal obligations from arbitrary fines and extractions.
He attributes many cultivator complaints to excessive additional demands, fines and invented exactions imposed beyond customary obligations.
The treatise discusses Fars governors paying pishkesh on the order of roughly fifty to one hundred thousand tomans.
Abdollah Khan argues that pishkesh to Tehran was not by itself the root cause of lower-level exactions because customary intermediary margins could remain even if pishkesh disappeared.
Abolishing a payment at the top of the fiscal chain does not, in Abdollah Khan's analysis, guarantee relief at the bottom.
His reform principle is that principal and supplementary obligations and dealings between each administrative layer should be explicitly limited and defined.
The treatise emphasizes predictable obligations and constrained discretionary authority more than a blanket reduction of all customary taxation.
notes: Archive synthesis of repeated explicit arguments.
